newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese foreign bond buying may slow in 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: Japanese foreign bond buying may slow in 1997/98.

text.p: Some major Japanese investors are planning to adopt a cautious approach to foreign bond investments in fiscal 1997/98 and slow down the pace of growth of the past few years, fund managers say.

Although investors are not expecting the dollar to fall significantly against the yen in the near term, they do not see it rising much further either, leading them to be more careful with their investment plans for the new fiscal year.
Nippon Life Insurance Corp, for one, is planning to slow down the brisk pace of growth of its foreign bond investments over the past few years.

"We might reduce the scale of our foreign bond investments next fiscal year, after total net foreign bond purchases of nearly one trillion yen ($8.2 billion) over the past two fiscal years," said Kazuhiko Sunagawa, chief manager of the finance and investment planning office at Nippon Life, a major domestic insurer.

The net value of the company's new foreign bond purchases totalled 400 billion yen ($3.30 billion) in fiscal 1995/96, and it planned to invest another 500 billion yen ($4.13 billion) in the current fiscal year ending March 31.
"We've been buying since the dollar was at the 80 yen level, so we are not in a rush to build up our foreign bond positions aggressively from this point," Sunagawa said.
"We'll be continuing to diversify our investments into foreign bonds, but the net buying volume may be below the amounts in 1995 and 1996," he said.
Nippon Life will maintain a stance of investing in bonds with maturities of up to three years, Sunagawa said, adding that about 80 percent of its foreign bonds are U.S. bonds.
Japanese investors are growing cautious over the dollar amid speculation that the U.S. monetary authorities will tighten credit in the not-too-distant future.

"Even though it is highly unlikely the dollar will sink towards 100 yen again, the outlook of the dollar is still unclear," a senior fund manager at another life insurance firm said. "With the dollar still standing above 120 yen and economic fundamentals in the United States changing, we have to be more cautious."
Investors expect the dollar to trade in a range of 120 yen to 125 yen in the longer term.
Foreign bond investments by Japanese investors are made in U.S. dollars because of the currency's high liquidity. Any appreciation of the dollar would result in income gains for dollar-based bonds.
Many investors have increased the proportion of foreign bonds in their portfolios in recent years, aiming for higher returns at a time of record low interest rates at home.

But they are not expected to return to the peak levels of the 1980s when total foreign bond holdings of Japanese life insurers amounted to about 20 percent of their total assets. Market sources now estimate that insurers' foreign bond holdings are equal to about five to six percent of their assets.

"Foreign bond holdings were trimmed down to as little as four percent when the dollar sank below 80 yen (in April 1995)," said Takashi Kawashima, manager of the investment planning division at Dai-Ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co.
"I think the foreign bond holding ratio will be kept below 10 percent," Kawashima said.

Dai-Ichi Life said it planned about 500 billion yen ($4.13 billion) worth of new foreign bond investment in fiscal 1996/97 on a net basis, but has yet to decide how much it will spend in the 1997/98 fiscal year.
"We are still in a phase of diversifying our investments into foreign bonds," Kawashima said. ($1=121 yen)
